item.title: Best Core Keeper Starting Seed — Seeds for a Smooth First Session (1.3.0.6)
item.description: A good starting seed buys you the first hour of Core Keeper: loot close to the Core, a peaceful meadow to grab early wool and milk, and no 20-tunnel dig just to find copper. This page lists the community-verified starting seeds we trust — every entry traces back to a Reddit, Discord or press roundup source. For how seeds actually shape your world, read the Seeds guide. Why we recommend these seeds Seed What you get Who it’s for 400957925946 Useful starter items near spawn First-timers who want a frictionless opening 1 Meadow sub-biome north of the Core Anyone who wants Moolin / Bambuck immediately 186511372992 Meadow sub-biome southeast of the Core Fallback if seed 1 feels cramped None of these “cheat” the game — they just put the fixed, seed-locked features (a meadow, starter chests) on a short leash from The Core.

item.title: Big Larva
item.description: The Big Larva is an aggressive hostile worm of The Clay Caves and the Larva Hive. It is a larger cousin of the common Larva and will chew through your base if left unchecked. Where to find it It spawns in The Clay Caves and the Larva Hive Biome, respawning on Chrysalis tiles. Combat tips Larva aggro on torches first — they prefer lit player objects over other targets, and will attack many player-placed base buildings Melee deals 93 damage with 412 HP; keep your distance and kite Immune to slow from slime and immune to acid damage Because it targets torches, it can be lured away from your camp Drops Larva Meat — 82.

item.title: Blackbug
item.description: Blackbug is a critter in Core Keeper. Unlike hostile mobs, critters are peaceful creatures you can catch with a Bug Net and keep or feed. Where to find it It frequently spawns when destroying wooden objects — breaking Wood, Coral Wood or Gleam Wood has a 15% chance to spawn one, while breaking wooden crates (such as Wooden Crates and Large Crates) has a 30% chance to spawn 1–2 (or 5–8 from large crates).

item.title: Blue Slime
item.description: Blue Slime is a hostile enemy mob in Core Keeper found in The Sunken Sea. It hops at you like other slimes, but its hits apply a slippery movement debuff that knocks both players and opposing mobs skidding across the ground. Where to find it It spawns naturally in The Sunken Sea, respawning periodically on Ground Slippery Slime tiles. Combat tips Stay off the slippery tiles when fighting: with 1,350 HP and 194 jump damage, it is far tougher than early slimes — don’t get knocked around on its home turf Slippery on hit: it knocks you back and applies slippery movement, which can slide you into other Sunken Sea hazards Immunities: immune to slime slow and slippery movement itself Drops Slippery Slime (94.

item.title: Bomb Scarab

It dives through players, then — once hurt badly enough — channels and detonates, breaking nearby walls and objects. Where to find it It spawns in The Desert of Beginnings, rarely respawning on Desert Sand Ground inside the desert biome. Scarab ambushes also burrow out of the ground in groups, and Ra-Akar the Sand Titan summons them as adds during the boss fight.

item.description: The Caveling Assassin is a fast Desert caveling that fires a spread of three daggers and then dashes straight through its target. Its high speed and pass-through movement make it hard to pin down. Tips Data sourced from the Core Keeper wiki (atma.gg); numbers shift with patches Bring appropriate resistance gear before farming this area

item.title: Caveling Brute
item.description: The Caveling Brute is a slow but hard-hitting melee enemy found in The Undergrounds and The Clay Caves. It hits much harder than a normal Caveling — don’t tank its swings. Combat tips Dodge, don’t block: its swings are telegraphed; sidestep rather than trading hits Kite it: it’s slower than the player, so attack between its swing cooldowns Iron gear comfort: with 140 HP and 16 damage, it’s manageable in copper but much safer in tin+ Drops Caveling Remains (common) — salvage/repair material Iron Ore (common) — early source before you reach The Forgotten Ruins

item.title: Caveling Gardener
item.description: The Caveling Gardener patrols Azeos’ Wilderness on Lush Moss, circling players before striking. While standing on grass it can sprout up to five Snare Plants that trap you in place. Tips Data sourced from the Core Keeper wiki (atma.gg); numbers shift with patches Bring appropriate resistance gear before farming this area

item.title: Caveling Hunter
item.description: Caveling Hunter is a hostile enemy mob in Core Keeper. These sneaky snipers temporarily disguise themselves as a Wilderness Bush, then snipe players with a Flintlock Musket from surprisingly long range — sometimes almost off-screen. Where to find it It spawns naturally in Azeos’ Wilderness, respawning periodically on Lush Moss tiles. Combat tips Watch the bushes: it pretends to be a bush until you get close — scan suspicious foliage before walking past Close the distance: it wants to keep range; the musket projectile is fast but the rate of fire is slow, so dash between shots Ranged answers work too: return fire from beyond its preferred musket band while it keeps kiting 870 HP, 152 range damage: don’t let it chip you from off-screen while you fight other mobs Drops Lush Moss (2.

item.title: Caveling Mummy
item.description: Caveling Mummy is a hostile enemy mob in Core Keeper. A mold-infected undead caveling wandering The Desert of Beginnings, it is best known for dropping the Zealot’s Scimitar, the Puppet Ring and the pajama clothing set. Where to find it It spawns in The Desert of Beginnings (mold-infected faction). Combat tips High health pool: 1,836 HP — expect longer fights than ordinary desert mobs Damage value: not listed on the wiki page (data待核) — treat it as a mid-tier desert threat and don’t face-tank unarmored Farm it for gear: its interesting drops (Zealot’s Scimitar, Puppet Ring, pajama set) sit around a ~2.

Tips Data sourced from the Core Keeper wiki (atma.gg); numbers shift with patches Bring appropriate resistance gear before farming this area

item.title: Caveling Spearman
item.description: Caveling Spearman is a hostile enemy mob in Core Keeper found in The Clay Caves. It is the close-quarters melee counterpart to the spear-throwing Caveling Skirmisher — a low-health early cave mob you will meet constantly while mining clay. Where to find it It spawns naturally in The Clay Caves, respawning on Clay Moss tiles. Combat tips Treat it as basic fodder: only 270 HP and a 74-damage melee hit — safe in copper gear once you understand its swing Don’t stand in clusters: Clay Moss spawns it alongside Skirmishers that throw spears from range; kite the group rather than face-tanking Cheap farm target: reliable early Larva Meat and Fiber source while exploring the caves Drops Fiber (22.

item.title: Core Keeper Accessories — Necklaces, Rings and Polished Gear
item.description: Accessories are the jewelry and bag slots that sit outside your armor set: a Necklace, a Ring and a Backpack slot. They are where builds actually get defined — armor gives stats, accessories give thematic effects: minion builds, fishing-as-range-damage, explosive crits, mana-barrier tanking, and pet buffs all live in jewelry. Most are crafted at the Jewelry Workbench (Iron Workbench tier) or the upgraded Proficient Jewelry Workbench, with polished versions available on early and mid-tier pieces.

item.title: Core Keeper Achievements
item.description: Achievements in Core Keeper are the Steam trophy trackers that shadow your run: roughly sixty trophies split between boss kills, skill masteries, rare collectibles and a handful of deliberately silly hidden tasks. Many show their condition up front, while the hidden ones stay blank until you stumble into them. How the list is structured Visible trophies hand you the objective in the Steam client; hidden trophies show only a name and an icon, so spoilers are built into the design.

item.title: Core Keeper Armor Guide — Set Bonuses and Damage Reduction
item.description: Armor is the three-piece defensive layer you wear on your head, chest and legs. Each piece adds a flat armor score plus a small sprinkling of offensive stats — max health, % damage, critical chance, attack speed — and matching pieces from the same set unlock set bonuses at 2, 3 or (rarely) 5 pieces. The trap for new players is treating armor as a raw number: the real defense math caps the benefit, which means piling more and more armor past a soft plateau buys almost nothing.

item.title: Core Keeper Automation — Electricity, Wires and Auto Farms
item.description: Automation is the set of powered machines that turn a base into a self-running factory: drills chew through Ore Boulders while you are off fighting, conveyor belts ferry dropped loot into chests, and Robot Arms pull items between inventories so you never have to walk back. Every electrical machine runs on a simple two-wire logic — a power source, a length of conducting wire, and whatever you want switched on the other end.

item.title: Core Keeper Automation Guide — Auto Farms, Drills and Power Circuits That Actually Work
item.description: Once your base has smelters and chests, the next time sink is feeding them. This automation guide goes past the basics: how power actually travels, which machines to put on the Automation Table, and four farm layouts — ore boulders, wood, crops and mobs — that run while you explore. How electricity really works Every automation machine needs a powered tile next to it (or a run of Electrical Wire). Powered machines show yellow notches on the four sides of their base.

item.title: Core Keeper Base Building Guide — Room Rules, NPC Housing and Automation
item.description: A good Core Keeper base is more than a pile of chests. This base building guide covers the room system, NPC move-in rules, bed mechanics and the automation basics that keep your underground hub running while you explore. Room rules that actually matter Rooms are the core building block of a Core Keeper base. The game recognizes a room when: The enclosed area is between 2×2 and 8×8 tiles (smaller or larger rooms don’t register) It has a door and a bed It contains the required item for the NPC you want (each NPC has a specific item) No players are within 30 tiles of the room for roughly a minute If any condition fails, the room won’t count — and NPCs won’t move in.

item.title: Core Keeper Biomes — Inner, Outer and Sub-Biomes Explained
item.description: Source: Biomes — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg) and World — Core Keeper Wiki, cross-checked against this site’s biome data. Distances are approximate tile counts from The Core. Biomes are the geometrically defined colour-coded zones of a Core Keeper world, each with its own terrain, ores, enemy roster, fish catches and native bosses. The layout is radial and deterministic: the ring distances are the same on every world, but the angular position of each biome is randomised by the seed.

item.title: Core Keeper Boss Fight Strategy — How to Beat Every Boss, Positioning and Gear
item.description: The boss guide covers where each boss lives, how to summon it and what it drops. This strategy guide is the fight itself: the health pools, the attack numbers, the enrage thresholds, and the positioning that turns a wipe into a farm. Rules that apply to almost every boss Enrage at a threshold. Most bosses switch to a faster, deadlier phase once you push them below a health percentage — the fight gets harder near the end, not easier.

item.title: Core Keeper Boss Guide — All 7 Bosses, Drops, Locations and Strategies
item.description: Core Keeper’s boss order follows your tool progression: three bosses around the Core must fall before it powers up, then the outer-ring titans open endgame content. This Core Keeper boss guide lists every boss, where they spawn, how to summon them and what they drop. The three early bosses (power up the Core) Defeat all three and place their drops on the effigies next to the Core to activate it.

item.title: Core Keeper Boss Mechanics — Summoning, Scanners and Respawns
item.description: Bosses are the large signature enemies that gate progression and mark biomes. They spawn at fixed distances from The Core at random angles, which means you can triangulate them by how far you have walked rather than memorising a seed. Every boss falls into one of three buckets: story bosses that drop the hearts and souls you need to power The Core and open new biomes, optional side bosses that farm materials and legendary recipes, and post-game bosses that unlock after the main story ends.

item.title: Core Keeper Co-op Guide — Multiplayer Scaling, Division of Labour and Shared Progress
item.description: Core Keeper is built for the couch-cave loop: three friends, one Core, nobody agreeing on where the farm goes. item.title: Core Keeper Cooking
item.description: Cooking is how you turn raw foraged ingredients into dishes that punch far above their weight. Dropping two ingredients into a Cooking Pot produces a meal with stronger buffs, longer duration, and hidden stat combinations you’d never see from eating them raw. Understanding the hidden math behind the pot is what separates a good survivor from an endgame-ready one. How the Cooking Pot works Set a Cooking Pot down on any flat surface, walk up to it, and interact to open its interface.

item.title: Core Keeper Cooking & Food Buff Guide — Best Recipes and How Buffs Stack
item.description: Food in Core Keeper isn’t just hunger — the right dishes are pre-boss loadouts. This cooking guide explains how food buffs work, which ingredients give the strongest effects, and the best combos before each fight. How food buffs work Food value refills your hunger; hunger loss only reduces max health and stats — you can’t die of starvation. Cooked ingredients give Regen, max health, armor, damage and speed buffs with a duration.

item.description: Crafting is how you turn raw ore, wood and drops into tools, armour, furniture and automation parts. Almost everything is made at a station you place in your base, although a handful of items can be crafted straight from your inventory. Stations form a long progression ladder: every new bench automatically carries over every recipe from the tier below, so you never have to rebuild an old recipe just because you unlocked a newer one.

item.description: Fishing is a leisure skill in Core Keeper that quietly pays for itself: toss a rod into any water tile, wait for a bite, and pull up fish, ore, kelp, loose tools or even locked chests. It also feeds the cooking loop, because a well-cooked fish dish hands you a real damage buff right before a boss attempt. item.title: Core Keeper Mechanics
item.description: Mechanics is the set of hidden formulas behind every number in Core Keeper: how your attacks scale, how much punishment your armour actually soaks, how power-ups wear off, and why bosses suddenly feel twice as scary with a friend online. Most players beat the early game by feel, but once you start min-maxing around Scarlet, Octarine and legendary gear, the order these bonuses apply decides whether a build is strong or merely okay.

item.title: Core Keeper Mining
item.description: Mining means breaking walls to dig out metal ore and other materials as you explore. Early on you chew through dirt, stone and ore veins by hand, but the real bottleneck is damage thresholds: every wall type absorbs a flat chunk of your mining power before your pickaxe starts actually chipping it. Once Drills unlock later, giant Ore Boulders become a far more efficient supply of metal — but until then, knowing which pickaxe to craft next is the single biggest speed-up available.

How wall damage really works A wall does not have a simple health bar. Every hit first deducts a flat resistance, and only the leftover damage bites into wall health.

item.description: Scenes are the hand-designed set pieces scattered across an otherwise procedural world. The tunnels, ores and dirt around you are generated algorithmically, but a shrine, a buried chest room, a merchant’s cell or a maze is a pre-built structure stamped into the map whole. Learning to recognize them by shape turns routine digging into targeted treasure hunting. item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Events
item.description: Seasonal events are short, theme-driven celebrations that transform the underworld for a few weeks every year — pumpkins in autumn, snow and presents in winter, cherry blossoms in spring. During each window, certain enemies and bosses get a visual reskin, the main-menu logo changes to match the theme, and a roster of exclusive food, vanity and building items becomes available. Most of that limited loot is sold by the travelling Seasonal Merchant, so collecting the full set depends on logging in at the right time.

item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Merchant — How to Summon and What They Sell
item.description: The Seasonal Merchant is the travelling vendor who shows up only during real-world celebrations — Halloween, Christmas, Easter and the rest. They do not wander in on their own; you have to invite them with a specific crafting item. Their stock is event-exclusive and is bought with event-specific currency, not ordinary coins, so missing the window means waiting a full year for the same items to return. item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Workbenches — Event-Only Crafting Stations
item.description: Each recurring celebration adds its own event-only workbench to the game. These benches are not part of the normal workbench ladder — they do not inherit recipes from the Copper/Tin/Iron tier, and they are not permanent unlocks. They exist only during their event window, are bought from the Seasonal Merchant, and vanish from the merchant’s stock when the celebration ends. Anything you have already crafted, however, stays in your storage forever.

item.title: Core Keeper Skills
item.description: Skills are your character’s passive progression track. Rather than spending points by hand, you earn experience simply by doing the activities the game already expects — swinging a pickaxe, swinging a sword, running around, planting seeds — and that experience slowly fills each skill bar toward level 100. Every discipline grants a small permanent bonus as it levels, and every fifth level hands you a talent point to spend in that skill’s own tree.

item.title: Core Keeper The Great Wall — The Outer Biome Gate
item.description: The Great Wall is an unbreakable, undulating ring of mechanical-looking blocks that separates the three inner biomes from the outer world. It is not a natural formation you can dig through — every tool, weapon and explosive bounces off it. It exists purely as a progression gate: until The Core lets you take it down, the Azeos’ Wilderness, the Sunken Sea and the Desert of Beginnings are off-limits no matter how far you walk.

item.title: Core Keeper World Generation — Chunks, Seeds and Terrain Pipeline
item.description: World generation in Core Keeper is layered rather than instant. When you create a world, the game bakes a deterministic seed value into the save, but the map itself is not built all at once. Empty tiles start as solid Obsidian Blocks and only turn into dirt, stone, water and dungeons as players trigger them. This page explains the pipeline: what is fixed at creation, what is rolled as you explore, and why two players on the same seed always see the same map.

item.title: Core Keeper World Seeds Guide — How Seeds Shape Your World
item.description: Every Core Keeper world is generated from a seed — the number you pick at world creation. The seed decides where each biome ring sits, which direction you find the Clay Caves, and roughly where the early bosses spawn. This guide explains how seed generation works and how to use seeds with friends. item.description: The Yellow Glowbug is a flying critter in Core Keeper. Unlike hostile mobs, critters are peaceful creatures you can catch with a Bug Net. This one drifts in swarms that look like dancing lights and glows yellow. Where to find it It appears in swarms in The Undergrounds, The Clay Caves, and The Desert of Beginnings. Its yellow glow is specific to these biomes. How to catch Equip a Bug Net and swing at it as you walk close It is stationary once placed, and emits yellow light — a free, slot-free light source for your base Caught glowbugs can be placed back in the world as persistent decoration, but they still move around and die in a single hit if attacked Sell value: 1 Feeding Glowbugs are the one critter cattle will not eat — Strolly Poly, Dodo, and Orex eat all critters except glowbugs, so keep them as lighting rather than feed.
